title: Is It Better to Read on Paper or an E-Reader?
author: Alex Quigley
summary: Alex Quigley synthesises new University of Valencia research spanning two decades of studies comparing print and digital reading, concluding that for text comprehension specifically, paper still tends to out-perform screens - but with an important age-dependent caveat. For primary-age children still learning to read, the research found a negative relationship between leisure digital reading and text comprehension, while for secondary and university-age students the relationship turned positive, suggesting older, more skilled readers can benefit from digital formats in ways younger readers cannot. Quigley attributes print's advantage partly to a 'deep reading mindset' - the more immersive, less interruption-prone experience of physical text compared to scrollable, clickable digital formats that risk disturbing careful reading. His practical guidance splits by age and purpose: young children should get heavy exposure to traditional print to build foundational 'print knowledge' before their reading diet is varied, while e-readers and audiobooks have a legitimate place for older, more established readers and for building reading habits through convenient alternative formats. Quigley explicitly warns against a reflexive 'Luddite attitude' that rejects digital reading tools outright, framing the real task as matching reading mode carefully to the reader's age, purpose, and stage of development.
points: The core research finding Quigley reports: a University of Valencia synthesis of two decades of research found print reading generally out-performs screen reading for text comprehension - but the effect is age-dependent.

The age-dependent split: primary-age children learning to read show a negative relationship between leisure digital reading and comprehension, while secondary and university-age students show a positive relationship.

Quigley's explanatory mechanism: a 'deep reading mindset' associated with traditional print is likely more immersive, while the ability to scroll and click in digital texts can disturb the careful, sustained attention that reading comprehension requires.

His practical age-based guidance: young children should get heavy exposure to traditional print to build foundational 'print knowledge' before diversifying into digital formats once they are established, skilled readers.

Quigley explicitly cautions against a 'Luddite attitude' rejecting e-readers and digital textbooks outright - e-readers and audiobooks have real value for engagement and habit-building, particularly for older readers and reluctant readers.
quotes: New research from the University of Valencia, Spain, has synthesised research from the last two decades and has found that when it comes to text comprehension -- reading to learn -- that print reading on paper may still be bettering glossy new screens.

When learning to read, such as in primary school, a negative relationship was observed between leisure digital reading and text comprehension. However, for secondary and university age students, the relationship turned into a positive one.
What the research indicates is that reading 10 hours of print on paper may prove more likely to be retained.
With digital texts, we can scroll and click, but that can potentially disturb the careful act of reading.
We should be wary of a Luddite attitude to technology that rejects e-readers or digital textbooks, but at the same time we should select our mode of reading with care.
When it comes to younger children, we should give them lots and lots of exposure to traditional print (thereby developing 'print knowledge').
